extracted.intended_audience: general readers, comedy fans, performers, critics and researchers interested in Stewart Lee or British stand-up
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of Stewart Lee's comedic techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the characteristics, techniques and practices used by Stewart Lee across his stand-up, television and writing — useful for performers, critics, and scholars studying alternative British comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up routine characterised by repetition, internal reference, and deadpan delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: His stand-up routine is characterised by repetition, internal reference, and deadpan delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summary statement (lead) defines the core audible/performative features that observers should expect in Lee's live work: repeated motifs, callbacks/internal referencing across a set, and a restrained, deadpan vocal style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition and internal reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition and internal reference are core elements of his material and set construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition and callbacks create an internal logic for the set that rewards attentive audiences; they are used to build momentum and irony rather than punchline-only laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Pull back and reveal" technique (conceal-then-reveal)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pull back and reveal" — the technique of concealing the true subject of a joke until the last moment, used to create comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lee notes this technique depends on English linguistic ambiguities and is harder to achieve in German. He links it to abandoning traditional joke-writing and to creating humour that pivots on late revelations of subject or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-humour and openly describing the structure/intent of the set
rubrics_metrics.description: He employs meta-humour, openly describing the structure and intent of the set while onstage, and abolishing the illusion of his routines as spontaneous acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves explaining or revealing the mechanics of the bit to the audience, using self-awareness as a source of comedy and undermining the 'this just happened' fiction that conventional stand-up often preserves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of onstage personae and ironic audience-criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee's delivery uses onstage personae, frequently alternating between an outspoken left-wing hero and that of a depressed failure and champagne socialist; he often criticises or scolds the audience (e.g., calling them a bias-seeking 'liberal intelligentsia').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching personae lets him satirise different positions and create ironic distance; scolding the audience becomes a deliberate tactic to frame material and test audience alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical, observational, self-deprecating and absurd subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: His comedy covers a wide range of forms and subject material. It is often topical, observational, self-deprecating and absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical themes include religion, political correctness and artistic integrity. Expect material rooted in current events or social observation, delivered with self-directed mockery and absurdist elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines culminating in feigned depressive episodes and nervous breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: His routines often culminate in feigned depressive episodes and nervous breakdowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These staged collapses operate as performance effects — part character work, part satire — and are used to punctuate or escalate the comic argument of a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation to investigate acceptability and highlight hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: He operates in a 'dangerous hinterland between moral provocation and outright offence', sometimes adopting the tactics of those he targets in order to highlight their hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Richard Hammond joke ('I wish he had been decapitated') and Lee's stated intent to probe boundaries of acceptability. The method intentionally courts controversy to expose double standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deconstruction as a comedic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of deconstruction (e.g., the Pea Green Boat show which deconstructed Edward Lear's 'The Owl and the Pussy-Cat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deconstruction reframes familiar texts or cultural objects to expose absurdities or create new comic narratives; it can be extended into longer-form material and adapted for radio/record releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on writing material about ideas rather than traditional joke-writing (translatability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee stated he had 'abandoned writing jokes in a traditional sense, instead focusing on writing humorous material about ideas which would be more easily translatable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach emphasizes concept-driven comedy (ideas-as-content) over set-up/punchline mechanics, partly motivated by working for German-language theatre where certain English wordplay is ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on English linguistic structures for humour (translation limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much British humour is dependent on the linguistic structures and vocabulary of English allowing for confusion among multiple meanings of statements or words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lee uses this observation to explain both his techniques (e.g., pull back and reveal) and the challenges of translating English wordplay; performers should be aware of language-specific devices when adapting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negative reviews and self-deprecation in marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: He frequently uses negative reviews on his posters to put off potential audience members who are unlikely to like his comedy style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit marketing tactic: repurposing criticism as a filter to attract the 'right' audience and discourage those who'd react negatively to his tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bringing moral issues in stand-up to public attention (ethics of writing/credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee has brought attention to issues such as uncredited writers, plagiarism and extremism in stand-up, comparing uncredited writing to athletes using performance-enhancing drugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutes a normative stance: expectations that stand-ups should write their own material or credit collaborators. It's a criterion for evaluating professional ethics in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and curation of alternative comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: He has produced and fronted showcases (e.g., The Alternative Comedy Experience) to promote creative/alternative comedy talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practice it signals a commitment to a particular aesthetic community; for evaluators, involvement in curation/production can be a metric of influence and support for alternative scenes.
